title: Network Denial of Service
summary: Network denial of service attacks attack availability by consuming the transport capacity that a service depends on, rather than the resources of the server itself. The mechanism is saturation: when offered traffic exceeds the bandwidth of the target link, or the capacity of the network devices in front of it, legitimate packets are dropped and users cannot reach the service even though the server is healthy. Practical variants include direct floods of raw packet volume, reflection and amplification that turn third-party servers into unwitting senders, and application protocol floods that consume connection state rather than link capacity. Two shared enablers recur throughout: source address spoofing, which hides the origin and makes address based filtering weak, and botnets, which spread small volumes across a very large number of hosts so that no single source looks abnormal. Detection therefore depends on flow level evidence rather than packet content. Useful signals are the sudden onset of a volume spike with an unusual protocol or flag mix, many sources contacting one destination with no returning session, response ratios far below normal, and traffic that reaches the target from reflector services the organisation does not normally use. Legitimate peaks such as a product launch or a marketing send have a business cause, a gradual ramp, and completed transactions; attack traffic usually does not. This technique sits alongside endpoint denial of service, which exhausts resources on the host once the traffic arrives.

beginner.definition: A network denial of service attack fills a network connection with traffic. Normal users cannot get through because the path is full. The service itself may be perfectly healthy. It is simply out of reach.
beginner.whyItMatters: When your website or email becomes unreachable, customers cannot buy, log in, or contact you. Even a short outage can cost money and damage trust. Attackers sometimes flood one system to distract your team while they break into another. The noise also makes it hard to tell a real attack from a busy day.
howItWorks: The attacker chooses a target service and works out how much bandwidth it has.
They generate traffic from one machine, or much more often from many machines.
The combined traffic is larger than the connection the target can carry.
Routers and firewalls drop packets, and they drop the packets from real users too.
Source addresses may be faked so you cannot simply block the sender.
Some attacks use other servers to send replies, hiding the true origin.
beginner.example: Picture a narrow street leading to a busy post office. A crowd is paid to stand in the street, not to enter the building. The post office staff are ready and the doors are open, but no real customer can reach the counter. Nothing inside the building is broken. The problem is the road, and that is exactly what a network flood does.
takeaways: This technique fills the network path, not the server's own resources.
Faked source addresses and botnets make simple blocking unreliable.
Watch for sudden volume changes and unusual protocol mixtures.

objectives: Define network denial of service and explain how saturation causes unavailability.
Distinguish network denial of service from endpoint resource exhaustion.
Describe how spoofed source addresses and botnets complicate defence.
Identify flow telemetry that indicates a flood in progress.
Explain how reflection and amplification differ from direct flooding.
Judge whether a traffic peak is legitimate demand or deliberate saturation.
